analysis.one_liner: Delays toxic air pollution limits for brick and clay kilns until court challenges finish.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; it cleared the Senate environment committee in September 2018 but died on the Senate calendar when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2015 the EPA set national limits on hazardous air pollutants — such as mercury and acid gases — from brick and structural clay kilns and clay ceramics plants. Existing plants were given deadlines to install controls. This bill would have pushed those deadlines back until courts finished reviewing legal challenges to the rule, or until December 26, 2020, whichever came first. The bill cleared committee but never came to a vote in the Senate, and the 2015 rules' deadlines stood.
analysis.who_benefits: Brick and structural clay products manufacturers and clay ceramics manufacturers would gain by putting off the cost of installing pollution controls on their kilns, and by having courts finish reviewing the rule before any spending is required. It would also shield plants that might close or shut down under the cost of compliance.

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the deadline for existing kilns to comply with EPA's 2015 hazardous air pollutant rules until the earlier of two years after all court judgments become final, or December 26, 2020 [S2][S3].

The extension applies to any kiln operator who filed a legal challenge during the 60-day window after the rule was published, letting judicial review run its course before compliance spending begins [S3].
If a court rules against EPA, the agency must issue new kiln emission regulations within one year of the litigation ending [S3].
The compliance delay also covers kilns owned by state, tribal, or local governments [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People living near brick and clay kilns would breathe hazardous air pollutants — the rules target mercury, acid gases, and other toxic emissions — for months or years longer than the original deadlines. The delay pushes the public-health benefits of the rule further into the future.

drawbacks.text: The core cost is delayed emission reductions: every month of the extension is another month that nearby residents are exposed to the hazardous air pollutants the 2015 rule was written to cut [S2].

The delay runs until the earlier of two years after all appeals conclude or December 26, 2020, so litigation timelines — which can stretch for years — determine how long plants keep operating under their old emission levels [S3].
A supporter would acknowledge the trade-off is direct: compliance costs for kiln owners are deferred only by postponing the pollution cuts the rule delivers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades real, if localized, public-health protection for compliance cost relief in a concentrated industry. The design gives kiln operators a predictable pause while courts rule, and requires EPA to redo the rule quickly if it loses in court, which is a legally tidy structure. But the cost falls on the communities around the kilns, who get the rule's pollution reductions later for no benefit of their own.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate environment committee approved it and set it on the Senate's calendar of pending business in September 2018, but the bill never came up for a floor vote and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Wicker introduced the bill on February 27, 2018 with five cosponsors from both parties [S1][S5].

The Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works reported it favorably without amendment on September 18, 2018, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 577 [S5].
A written committee report was filed on December 4, 2018, with minority views filed by committee members who disagreed [S5].
No vote ever occurred in the Senate, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the 2015 EPA emission deadlines stayed in place and kiln operators had to comply as scheduled. Communities near kilns came out ahead; the bill's industry backers did not get their compliance delay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near kilns, not the industry

industries.industry: Brick and structural clay products manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would defer the deadline for kilns to install controls for hazardous air pollutants, saving operators compliance costs and the risk of closure while courts review the rule. The public-health benefits of the 2015 rule would be postponed, so the industry's gain in this bill runs against nearby residents' interest.
The same EPA rule covers clay ceramics manufacturing, so those plants would get the identical compliance delay and cost deferral.
